# PWM voltage control of inverters

*Lecture 3 · EEU 08104 Power Electronics Design*

In many industrial applications the output voltage of an inverter must be controlled.

- The output can be varied by varying the **DC source voltage**, for example with a phase-controlled rectifier. The six-step inverter works this way: simple inverter control, at the cost of a variable DC source.
- When the DC source cannot be varied, or the losses of that stage cannot be tolerated, the inverter itself must vary the output. A **pulse-width modulation (PWM)** inverter does this, so a variable DC source is no longer needed.

**Principle.** A **reference signal** $A_r$ (constant or sinusoidal, at the desired output frequency) is compared with a repetitive **triangular carrier** $A_c$ at the switching frequency. The comparison (in a microcontroller or a comparator) generates the switching signals:

- $V_{ref} > V_{carrier}$: switch **on**;
- $V_{ref} < V_{carrier}$: switch **off**.

## Single-pulse-width modulation

- There is **one pulse per half cycle**, and its width $\delta$ is varied to control the output voltage.
- The gate signals come from comparing a **rectangular** reference of amplitude $A_r$ with a triangular carrier of amplitude $A_c$.
- Varying $A_r$ from 0 to $A_c$ varies the pulse width $\delta$ from 0° to 180°.
- The control variable is the **modulation index** $M = \dfrac{A_r}{A_c}$.

**Full bridge:** $A_r > A_c$ turns S1 and S2 on (output $+V_d$); during the other half cycle S3 and S4 are on (output $-V_d$). **Half bridge:** S1 on gives $+V_d/2$, S2 on gives $-V_d/2$; the gating signals are the same.

**rms output voltage** (pulse of width $\delta$ centred on $\pi/2$):

$$V_o = \left[\frac{2}{2\pi}\int_{(\pi - \delta)/2}^{(\pi + \delta)/2}V_d^2\,d(\omega t)\right]^{1/2} = V_d\sqrt{\frac{\delta}{\pi}}$$

**Fourier series:**

$$v_o(t) = \sum_{n = 1,3,5,\ldots}\frac{4V_d}{n\pi}\sin\frac{n\delta}{2}\sin n\omega t$$

*Example (added):* with $V_d = 220$ V and $\delta = 120°$, $V_o = 220\sqrt{2/3} = 179.6$ V and the rms fundamental is $\dfrac{4 \times 220}{\sqrt2\pi}\sin60° = 171.5$ V. The third harmonic vanishes, since $\sin(3 \times 60°) = 0$.

## Multiple-pulse-width modulation

- The harmonic content of single-pulse PWM is reduced by using **several pulses in each half cycle** (also called uniform PWM).
- The gate signals come from comparing a reference (a constant) with a triangular carrier.
- The **reference frequency** sets the output frequency $f_o$; the **carrier frequency** $f_c$ sets the number of pulses per half cycle:

$$P = \frac{f_c}{2f_o}$$

- The **modulation index** controls the output voltage. Varying $M$ from 0 to 1 varies the pulse width from 0 to $\pi/P$, and the output from 0 to $V_d$.
- With pulse width $\delta$, the rms output voltage is

$$V_o = \left[\frac{2P}{2\pi}\int_{(\pi/P - \delta)/2}^{(\pi/P + \delta)/2}V_d^2\,d(\omega t)\right]^{1/2} = V_d\sqrt{\frac{P\delta}{\pi}}$$

## Sinusoidal PWM (SPWM)

- Instead of keeping all pulses the same width, the width of each pulse is varied **in proportion to the amplitude of a sine wave** evaluated at the centre of the same pulse.
- It is the type commonly used in industry, because the **lower-order harmonics are reduced significantly**.
- The reference frequency $f_r$ sets the output frequency $f_o$; the carrier frequency is $f_c$; the reference amplitude $A_r$ sets the modulation index $M = A_r/A_c$ and so the **rms output voltage**.

A<tspan dy="4" font-size="10">c</tspan><tspan dy="-4"> (dashed), reference A</tspan><tspan dy="4" font-size="10">r</tspan></text><text x="560" y="173" text-anchor="end" class="d-t s a">v<tspan dy="4" font-size="10">AO</tspan></text></svg><figcaption>Sinusoidal PWM with bipolar switching (M = 0.8, 9 carrier cycles per output cycle). The switch S1 is on while A<sub>r</sub> > A<sub>c</sub>; the pulses are widest where the sine is largest, so the average of v<sub>AO</sub> follows the reference.</figcaption></figure>

- One leg: $A_r > A_c$ turns **S1** on; $A_r < A_c$ turns **S4** on. The two cannot be on at the same time, so $v_{AO}$ switches between $+\frac12V_d$ and $-\frac12V_d$.
- Second leg: $A_r > A_c$ turns S2 on; $A_r < A_c$ turns S3 on.
- The full-bridge output $v_{AB} = v_{AO} - v_{BO}$ switches between $+V_d$ and $-V_d$; a half bridge switches between $\pm\frac12V_d$. The analysis is the same for both.
- **Bipolar** means the switches in both legs switch **simultaneously** (S1 with S2, S3 with S4).

### Unipolar voltage switching

- The switches in the two legs are **not** switched simultaneously. Legs A and B are controlled separately, by comparing $A_c$ with $A_r$ and with $-A_r$.
- Leg A: $A_r > A_c$ turns S1 on and $v_{AN} = V_d$; $A_r < A_c$ turns S4 on and $v_{AN} = 0$ (N is the negative rail).
- Leg B: $-A_r > A_c$ turns S3 on and $v_{BN} = V_d$; $-A_r < A_c$ turns S2 on and $v_{BN} = 0$.
- So $v_{AB} = v_{AN} - v_{BN}$ steps between $+V_d$ and 0 in one half cycle and between 0 and $-V_d$ in the other. *(Added:* the output switches at twice the carrier frequency, so the harmonics move higher and are easier to filter.)

### Fourier coefficients

For either scheme the output is $v(t) = \displaystyle\sum_{n = 1,3,5,\ldots}\left(A_n\cos n\omega t + B_n\sin n\omega t\right)$.

**Bipolar:** let the $m$th positive pulse start at $\alpha_m$ with width $\delta_m$, followed by a negative pulse of width $\beta_m$. For each pair,

$$a_n = \frac{2V_d}{\pi}\left[\int_{\alpha_m}^{\alpha_m + \delta_m}\cos n\omega t\, d\omega t - \int_{\alpha_m + \delta_m}^{\alpha_m + \delta_m + \beta_m}\cos n\omega t\, d\omega t\right]$$

$$b_n = \frac{2V_d}{\pi}\left[\int_{\alpha_m}^{\alpha_m + \delta_m}\sin n\omega t\, d\omega t - \int_{\alpha_m + \delta_m}^{\alpha_m + \delta_m + \beta_m}\sin n\omega t\, d\omega t\right]$$

**Unipolar:** let the $i$th positive pulse start at $\alpha_i$ and end at $\alpha_i + \delta_i$; its negative partner starts at $\alpha_i + \pi$. For each pair,

$$a_n = \frac{2V}{\pi}\int_{\alpha_i}^{\alpha_i + \delta_i}\cos n\omega t\, d(\omega t), \qquad b_n = \frac{2V}{\pi}\int_{\alpha_i}^{\alpha_i + \delta_i}\sin n\omega t\, d(\omega t)$$

Adding all $P$ pulses:

$$A_n = \sum_{i = 1}^{P}\frac{2V}{n\pi}\left[\sin n(\alpha_i + \delta_i) - \sin n\alpha_i\right], \qquad B_n = \sum_{i = 1}^{P}\frac{2V}{n\pi}\left[\cos n\alpha_i - \cos n(\alpha_i + \delta_i)\right]$$

> **Correction to the lecture slides.** The single-pulse slide says "by varying $A_c$ from 0 to $A_c$"; it is the **reference** amplitude $A_r$ that is varied from 0 to $A_c$.
